title: How To Find Mysidia In Final Fantasy: Resonance
summary:
Final Fantasy: Resonance grants you an airship around halfway through its main story, giving you the ability to fly nearly anywhere you'd like across the world map. However, not too long after finally taking to the skies, you'll need to find the hidden city of Mysidia.

Finding Mysidia can prove frustrating if you're not quite sure what area to be looking in. Lucky for you, in this guide, we'll fill you in on exactly where to find Mysidia in Final Fantasy: Resonance.

Where to find Mysidia in Final Fantasy: Resonance

When you start Chapter 5 of Final Fantasy: Resonance, you'll need to discover the hidden city of Mysidia. To do so, you'll need to use a newly equipped radar system that has been attached to your airship. When you're flying around the world map, you can press the right trigger to send out a ping, and Lid will comment whether or not it's picking up any traces of Mysidia.

You can fly around the map pinging randomly until Lid starts noticing traces, then follow her directions, but that can prove slightly frustrating. If you'd rather skip the search, we'll simply tell you how to find Mysidia.

To find Mysidia, head to the very southern portion of the map. Note the large mass of the Kingdom of Pharm (left) and two small islands seen in the photo above. Pass between the landmasses and head slightly further south, then use your ping to unveil Mysidia.

Later in the game, this pinging radar system comes into play again to aid you in finding treasure across the world map. As with finding Mysidia, you'll just need to fly around pinging until Lid picks up on something, then follow her guidance to help you round up some fresh loot. Happy hunting!

Final Fantasy: Resonance is available now on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC. For more on this HD-2D JRPG, you can check out how long it takes to beat Final Fantasy: Resonance to see how much more of the journey lies ahead.

title: Final Fantasy Resonance’s First Boss Will Give You Hell Unless You Grab These Key Items
summary:
You'll come up against a handful of tutorial bosses during Chapter 1 of Final Fantasy: Resonance's lengthy adventure. However, none will pose nearly the challenge of its first esper boss, Siren, whom you'll find awaiting you at the top of her spiral tower.

This tough opponent can hit hard and cast Charm on your party, which certainly poses a problem if you're not prepared to deal with it. But don't worry, as we've got some tips for dealing with Siren below.

How to beat Siren in Final Fantasy: Resonance

When Siren reaches around half health, she'll begin using an attack called Allure, which will immediately cast Charm on your entire party. Charm causes your characters to attack one another, which can cause damage to add up quickly. If you aren't prepared to combat Charm casts--on Normal or Expert difficulty especially--there's a reasonable chance Siren will get the best of your party.

Luckily, there are three ways you can prepare to nullify this annoying effect ahead of time--though there's definitely one that stands above the rest, which we'll tell you about at the end of this list.

  • Monk's Prayer Beads - This accessory nullifies Charm on whoever is wearing it. You can purchase two of these from the armor merchant in Granport Harbor for 1,500 gil each, or you can obtain them naturally. One can be easily found in a chest on your way up the tower to the boss, while another can be obtained by completing the very straightforward Secrets Unearthed sidequest from Chloe in Felicitas.
  • Equipping Leah - You can grant one character Charm immunity by simply having Leah equipped to them. Her "Nullify Charm" passive assures at least one party member is safe, and we'd recommend that be Fina if necessary. Read on for why that is.
  • Esuna or Pray - Esuna is a spell that can cure any ailment, and Pray is an ability that does the same thing. Since Siren can occasionally cast Silence on a character, Pray becomes unusable. Having Leah equipped on Fina is the best bet for this option, as she'll have access to Pray even if she's Silenced. In this case, you can quickly remove Charm from any party member who has been affected.

Of the options above, you'd ideally want to obtain three Monk's Prayer Beads (buy at least one and find two), allowing you to equip the Tronn to Fina instead. Tronn will allow her to use Lightning spells, which, as we're about to find out, is very useful.

Become the storm (as in, cast a lot of lightning)

Siren is weak to Lightning spells, which means you'll likely want to bring along a character with Tronn equipped that you can repeatedly blast Siren with the Thunder spell.

While you can equip Tronn to Lasswell (since they're both Breakers), it's ideal to have Cloud equipped to Lasswell and Tronn equipped to Fina. This allows both characters to have access to Lightning-based spells (Tronn's Thunder and Cloud's Thunder Surge). Meanwhile, Rain should keep Warrior of Light equipped so that he can keep unleashing Thunder Blade when able.

When you get off a beautiful Sweeping Stagger and have an opportunity to really lay into Siren, you'll also get the option to use a Resonance skill. Always use Ascension (Cloud's ability), as its massive Lightning damage will put a significant dent in Siren's health bar.

The rest is by the books

Beyond knowing how to nullify Charm and exploiting Siren's weaknesses, the remainder of the fight is fairly straightforward. The main thing to note is that you'll want to be level 11 or higher before facing her. Going into the fight at a lower level puts you at a significant disadvantage, both in terms of damage taken and your ability to stagger her quickly.

Siren doesn't have any particularly high damage attacks, though multiple hits without some healing can add up. Make sure to have one or two of your characters keeping enough MP aside for topping you all off as needed.

Siren will sometimes cast Silence, and if it manages to affect one of your characters, you'll be unable to use magic spells for two rounds. Make sure you've got some Potions handy to stay healed up during rough patches.

If you're prepared for this fight, it's not particularly difficult to come out victorious. And once you do, you'll gain access to Siren as an esper you can summon to fight alongside you in future battles. Awesome.

Final Fantasy: Resonance is available now on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC.

title: How Long Is Final Fantasy: Resonance – Chapter List And Total Hours
summary:
Final Fantasy: Resonance is the first HD-2D entry in Square Enix's long-running role-playing franchise, offering players a way to experience something both classic and new at the same time. With a story and gameplay mechanics that find a unique way to blend classic characters with an all-new cast, this one's no doubt a great spot for new players and returning fans to jump in.

If you're wondering how long it takes to see this HD-2D journey through, though, we've got you covered. Here's how long it takes to beat Final Fantasy: Resonance.

In This Article
  • How long it takes to beat Final Fantasy: Resonance
  • Final Fantasy: Resonance chapter list

How long it takes to beat Final Fantasy: Resonance

An average playthrough of Final Fantasy: Resonance takes around 30-40 hours. This includes seeing the core story through while doing a handful of side quests, plus some optional objectives like finding Visions, espers, and more.

This makes it a fairly hefty JRPG experience right out of the gate, but completionists will find that their playtime can be extended by nearly double if going for 100%. Especially for those seeking to obtain every trophy or achievement, Final Fantasy: Resonance can easily take 70+ hours to see and do everything it has to offer.

Of course, those who want to mainline the story, or who opt to play on Casual difficulty, may reach the game's conclusion more quickly. Meanwhile, choosing the hardest difficulty may add enough challenge that you could see your playtime exceed 80 hours.

How you decide to experience Final Fantasy: Resonance is entirely up to you, so play it on the difficulty that feels right. And there's no need to feel obligated to see and do everything, as you can mostly just engage with the parts that you enjoy along the way to seeing how the game's epic story concludes.

Final Fantasy: Resonance chapter list

Final Fantasy: Resonance is split into eight chapters, which play out linearly. While you can stop and smell the roses (as in, do plenty of side quests and more), these chapters represent the arcs of the game's main story.

  1. Tailing the Truth
  2. Eternal Blue
  3. Wardens of the Aquapolis
  4. Banner Oath
  5. Scars of Time
  6. Tranquility
  7. Reckoning
  8. Beyond Hope

In addition to the main chapters of Final Fantasy: Resonance, you can find a bevy of side quests to complete throughout the game's sprawling world. They're usually worth doing, too, as they frequently grant above-average gear for your characters, which will help you tackle upcoming battles more easily.

Final Fantasy: Resonance is available now on PS5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC.

title: In Final Fantasy: Resonance, Take This Early Detour To Unlock Cloud Strife
summary:
Few characters in the Final Fantasy series are as recognizable and universally adored as Cloud Strife from Final Fantasy VII. So, it makes sense that Final Fantasy: Resonance would include the snarky mercenary in its cast of Visions, which function as equippable characters that aid your party.

If you're looking to get your hands on Cloud as soon as possible, you'll be happy to hear that this popular spiky-haired fellow can be added to your party within the first few hours of the game. Here's how to get Cloud in Final Fantasy: Resonance.

How to get Cloud Strife in Final Fantasy: Resonance

As with all Visions in Final Fantasy: Resonance, obtaining Cloud requires you to visit his respective sanctum in the overworld. Luckily, for fans of this beloved hero, the Sanctum of Cloud becomes available quite early in the adventure during Chapter 1. However, it requires a bit of a detour, which means you could potentially miss it if you're not thoroughly exploring.

After the initial events at the Earth Shrine play out, you'll soon find yourself journeying to the desert in the west. It's in this area of the overworld that you'll find the Sanctum of Cloud, but you'll want to wrap up your brief visit to the Village of Kol first. You won't be able to reach the sanctum from this side of the desert.

Instead, wait until you've made your way all the way to the west of this portion of the continent to reach Grandport Harbor. You'll be spending quite a bit of time there for the main story, but for now, we'll just use it as a starting point for our journey to the Sanctum of Cloud.

From Grandport Harbor, head north, then take the bridge slightly to the east. Immediately after crossing over the sand waterfall on the other side, head all the way north. Pass the cave here and wrap around south to spot the Sanctum of Cloud.

Refer to the map above for the exact location of the Sanctum of Cloud.

Inside Cloud's Sanctum, simply approach and interact with the crystal at the end of the path. You'll be given a fairly lengthy explanation of Cloud as a character, and you'll be asked to answer three questions pertaining to his story. How you answer these questions has no effect on anything, so just choose the ones that feel right to you.

When you've answered all three questions, you'll receive Cloud as a Vision, allowing you to equip and use him in battle.

Cloud is a Breaker, meaning the character you equip him to will start learning additional abilities that aid in staggering enemies and dealing massive damage to them. Pairing him with Lasswell is the best bet early on, as he is also a Breaker, and he can quickly become a staggering powerhouse once he's got Cloud working alongside him.

Also, Cloud has an incredibly powerful Resonance attack called Ascension that is exceptional against single targets--especially those weak to Lightning. You'll want to keep this in mind when facing off against Chapter 1's most formidable boss, Siren.

title: EA Cancels New Mass Effect, Pauses New Sims Game, And All The Other  Big EA News That Just Happened
summary:
When EA was acquired by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, many expected major changes at the gaming company, including layoffs and game cancellations, among other shakeups. Now, those have begun, with EA on October 21 confirming a series of significant changes impacting the people and teams that worked on many storied franchises.

EA also teased some of what's to come in the future, including a joint project between Respawn and DICE. Here's a rundown of all the big EA news today.

Layoffs

EA said in a statement that it made the "difficult" choice to lay off staff, and Bloomberg reported that the cuts will impact about 400 people. Affected staffers will be treated with "care and respect," EA said, and some impacted employees may have a chance to get a different job within EA. Alongside the BioWare closure noted below, staff at Ripple Effect (Battlefield), Maxis (The Sims), and Full Circle (Skate) have been impacted, as noted by Vertical Slice.

BioWare closes and new Mass Effect axed

BioWare, the esteemed Canadian developer founded 30+ years ago, is shutting down. The studio employed fewer than 100 people, Bloomberg reported, and the team was working on the next Mass Effect. That game is now canceled.

"BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly," EA said.

Developers at BioWare had feared their jobs were at risk after PIF announced that it would buy EA. BioWare is known, in part, for making pro-diversity games featuring inclusive storytelling and characters.

Longtime BioWare writer Patrick Weekes, who was laid off in 2025, speculated that EA’s new owners, including the PIF, might want to avoid “gay stuff” and politics that the PIF’s leadership does not agree with.

There has been an outpouring of support and thoughtful messages about BioWare in the wake of the news, from fans and industry professionals alike.

CD Projekt's Michal Nowakowski said his company first got to know BioWare when the studio did the work to localize Baldur's Gate games in Europe. Later, BioWare lent its game engine to CD Projekt for the first Witcher game.

"Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry," he said.

New The Sims game paused

Another game that's not going ahead at EA is Project Lotus, the codename for new game in The Sims franchise. Another The Sims game, codename Project Evergreen, is now the main focus for the developers working on The Sims. Exactly what this game is, however, remains a mystery, but The Sims is a juggernaut at EA and fans have been waiting for a new game for a long time.

Skate gets scaled back

EA's new Skate game, which was released in 2025, will remain online, but EA said it's "making changes to the studio," and that includes cutting staff to create a "more focused, smaller team." EA said this will help Skate have a "very clear roadmap" and one that can lead to a "healthier and more sustainable business."

EA Sports open-world football game

The EA Sports division, which is among the strongest at the company due in part to the lucrative loot boxes and microtransactions in Ultimate Team modes, continue to operate "from a position of strength," EA said. In addition to the usual annual sports games, EA said it has two new projects in the works, including a "brand-new, social-first open-world" football game in the works under the codename Project Gridiron. The other project is the next Fight Night, which is coming back after a 15-year hiatus.

Shooters

EA said Battlefield 6 was a "great success," and that the studio "learned a lot from the launch and live service." There will be future Battlefield games, as well as a new project to be collaboratively developed by Respawn and DICE. EA didn't say what this will be, but many believe it could be a new Star Wars: Battlefront, following recent rumors that DICE could make that game. Variety reported that yes, indeed, a new Battlefront game is coming. This would not be surprising at all, given DICE's two previous Battlefront games sold a combined 33 million+ copies.

As for Apex Legends, EA said it will continue to "invest heavily" in the franchise by adding new gameplay modes and "other new experiences."

Iron Man and Star Wars Jedi

While EA may have canceled its Black Panther game already, the company's other big Marvel game, Iron Man, remains in development. Additionally, the next Star Wars Jedi game is still on the way, EA confirmed.

"Beyond that, we will concentrate our efforts on fewer simultaneous, large-scale projects, ensuring that every game we build in this space is fully set up for success," EA said.

The biggest leveraged buyout of all time

The PIF, along with Silver Lake and Affinity Partners, took EA private in a $55 billion sale that was constructed as a leveraged buyout, or LBO. This was the largest LBO ever, not just in gaming, but in the history of all business. Since the acquisition was "leveraged," that means it comes with debt, and a lot of it, so many expected EA to make major cuts to help service that debt.

Prior to the deal closing, Piers Harding-Rolls of Ampere Analysis said EA may look to “cut excess spending and rationalize the company’s workforce” to help bring in more money to address the debt. A report from Financial Times said EA might look to further bolster AI tools and technologies to help cut development costs and drive profitability.

Mat Piscatella of Circana told GI.biz that the companies being acquired in LBOs rarely fare well. “Leveraged buyouts have a certain history that generally hasn’t been great for the acquired companies,” he said.

title: Your Favorite Video Games Will Always Be Influenced By Manga
summary:
In the heart of Brooklyn, there is now a devastatingly gorgeous manga panel from Jiro Taniguchi's Ice Age: Chronicle of the Earth hung on a gallery wall. I can't tell you what it says--I fear my scant familiarity with Japanese doesn't extend to literacy in kanji--but I can tell you what it portrays: a cityscape consumed by nature. A lush tangle of vines and trees reclaiming the Earth from its disastrous, mettlesome inheritors. 

While I doubt this panel and manga are the first time this kind of image has cropped up, it certainly feels like a progenitor to many similar visuals across the years. Your mind might jump to I Am Legend, the Will Smith-led feature film about a post-apocalyptic New York City, for example. My mind jumped straight to Nier Automata's city that's been lost to time, as well as The Last of Us' many dilapidated small towns and US metropolises. Though I went into the Brooklyn Museum's new Art of Manga exhibit already curious about what connections the form might have to games, it became quickly apparent that manga has always been in conversation with other mediums, influencing everything from anime to gaming.

The Brooklyn Museum, located right near Prospect Park in New York City, is currently home to the Art of Manga exhibit. Curated by Nicole Coolidge Rousmaniere--whose love of manga stems from early exposure to French graphic novels and reading Astro Boy at a seminal age--the gallery features a beautiful selection of Taniguchi’s work, as well as select other notable mangaka (manga artists and authors) of outsized influence. This includes Rumiko Takahashi, best known for her work on Ranma ½ and Inuyasha, Eiichiro Oda, the renowned creator of One Piece, and Hirohiko Araki, whose gorgeously styled illustrations from Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure are among the exhibits crown jewels. 

In total, the exhibit draws from the work of 10 mangaka, evenly split between male and female authors of varying popularity and prefectures of Japan, and explores different kinds of subject matter including inner-city living and queer life. This was essential to Rousmaniere, As she explained, "If I had featured fewer artists, the exhibition would not have been as powerful; We might not have gotten across the incredible range of these artists and the power of the line that they employ." The Art of Manga exhibit, evidently, needed to be big. 

And big it is. At its center, there is a reading room with bookshelves full of manga related to the artists spotlighted in the exhibit. Whole walls are adorned with iconic illustrations of some of the manga (a particularly poignant scene from One Piece comes to mind near the exhibit's end), but some of the highlighted art is also quite grand. Jojo's Bizarre Adventure, for example, is the subject of what Rousmaniere calls "the heart of the exhibition:" a 12-panel composition called "There is always a Traitor." The work consists of a series of life-sized panels of Jojo’s Bizarre Adventure’s Stand users assembled in tableau, with each panel towering over the average visitor and making the cast out to be even larger than life than they typically are. Or as Rousmaniere puts it, Araki's "2D figures are in fact 3D, and jump from the page into our imagination."

"What I adore about Araki Hirohiko is his versatility and his ability to embrace new challenges, be it life-size painting or lithography, fashion, or music. He has no bounds on his imagination and I think this is what makes him and his work so vital," Rousmaniere extolled.

A little ways away from that massive installation is a smaller piece from Araki that might look strikingly similar to many gamers. In it, many characters from Jojo's Bizarre Adventure stand huddled up on what appears to be a bus. The distinct juxtaposition of the cast's bright colors and exotic patterns against the drab gray of the bus interior cuts an imposing image. To the eye of your average RPG player, like me, the ensemble might look eerily close to that of a Persona game.

If you’re anything like me, you probably can’t look at Araki’s work without immediately drawing connections to Persona, a beloved RPG series from Atlus that touts, among many other things, an impeccable sense of forward-thinking fashion and style on par with the closets of characters like Jotaro and Jolyne.  

But that’s not all they have in common. The two also share a penchant for the supernatural and mythological, and both casts can summon powerful beings in battle. In the manga of JJBA, these forces are known as Stands, but in the world of Persona, they are called … well, Persona. The creators of the Persona games have never outright confirmed the influence of JJBA on the production of the series, but their lineage feels like an unspoken truth.

Manga's influence on games doesn't begin or end there, either. The mangaka of Dragon Ball, the late Akira Toriyama, literally helped sculpt the visual identity of both the Dragon Quest series and Chrono Trigger, two early successes for the companies that were then known separately as Square and Enix. Beyond that, it feels like the sensibilities and attitudes of these games and that era of RPG--the fascination with small-town living and domesticity for example--owe something to the genial nature of Toriyama's characters and the warm fantasy tapestry he helped to create.

Alternatively, much later RPGs feel like direct descendants of Berserk, the late Kentaro Miura’s manga, which has been a huge influence in the rise of dark fantasy. Miura's bleak fantasy epic has long served as a muse of sorts for a whole class of character in the Final Fantasy series, and has also been a major touchstone for From Software’s oeuvre like Dark Souls and Elden Ring. 

Of course, manga has also paved the way for anime, which often reimagines and reinterprets manga and has made global phenomena of many works, such as One Piece. One Piece has become one of the best-known brands since its anime adaptation enraptured the world, and now there are One Piece nights at baseball games! I can’t walk to one of my local trains without seeing a plush of Chopper in a neighbor’s window or a straw-hat ornament on a passerby's bag. And when you see Oda’s art on display in Brooklyn Museum’s exhibit, including an illustration that explicitly features Nami and Usopp playing video games featuring some very familiar caricatures, it’s easy to see why the series and its cast have inspired such awe across the world and artistic mediums.

The camaraderie between Luffy and his friends, which serves as the emotional core of the series, is aspirational and has seemingly served as the template for one of gaming’s more recent band of oddities. In an interview with Crunchyroll, the newest head of Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio (and longtime writer) Masayoshi Yokoyama admitted that the cast of Yakuza: Like a Dragon, the game that transformed the brawler series into a turn-based RPG, was molded after Luffy and the Straw Hat Pirates. 

Yokoyama told Crunchyroll at the time, "To me, Ichiban is basically Luffy. And around him there’s Zoro and Nami and basically the rest of the party, you know? One Piece’s party composition was on my mind so much during writing that it was a massive influence." It feels like Yokoyama's only scratching the surface with that comparison too. As two long-running series that often painstakingly shift perspectives to illuminate struggles against unfair systems and institutions, I don’t think it’s the only way that the two are alike.

Even if it is indirect, or I guess roundabout in this case, manga's force has become increasingly undeniable over the years. Rousmaniere shared, "When I was in Japan in the '80s, everyone was reading manga. I was studying archaeology and the archaeologists mostly all read manga. Manga captures the zeitgeist of a moment that other forms do not in a tangible, and not fleeting, fashion." As it's bled into anime with increasing success, manga's influence has only grown. Now it is, per Rousmaniere, "in Barnes and Noble in the US, in Waterstones in the UK, and in airports around the country." It's everywhere.

Though the Art of Manga exhibit may not overtly draw attention to the forms’ ties to games, there is one outstanding reference to the modern gaming landscape that’s hard to ignore. Before you enter the exhibit, right outside the entrance to Brooklyn Museum’s gift shop that is now itself adorned with manga-inspired merch and paraphernalia, there is an army of gashapon ("gacha") machines that visitors are encouraged to play. I clocked everything from Digimon to My Hero Academia and more among the capsule-sized toys and charms that players could pull. 

"Many people watch gamers just as I enjoy watching visitors and museum workers choosing their gashapon at the front of the store," Rousmaniere shared, drawing an interesting line from her enjoyment of seeing people turn their fascination with manga into a literal keepsake to how one might enjoy watching a streamer try pulling a legendary roll in a gacha game like Genshin Impact. That gashapon machines, whose mechanics have become the basis for countless popular video games in the last decade, just so happen to be halfway between manga and gaming makes their prominent inclusion here quite serendipitous. 

My big takeaway from the Art of Manga exhibit? Art goes beyond frames and borders, touches other artists and mediums outside of itself all the time, and continues spreading regardless of genres, nations, or any other manner of restraint. In some ways, you can draw an incredibly clear line from manga to games, like Araki's work and something like Persona. In other ways, the influence might be felt but not obviously seen. But it's always worth exploring other forms and, for instance, walking through a gallery like this one and interrogating where it all might stem from.

Brooklyn Museum's Art of Manga exhibit runs from October 3, 2026 to January 31, 2027.

title: Max Miller’s Tasting History Is Coming To Your Tabletop With A New Board Game
summary:
Behind his cheerful delivery and presentation, it turns out that Max Miller, known for turning historical recipes into entertaining yet educational YouTube lessons with his show Tasting History, is also quite serious about board games. Now, game designer Michael Shinall (Marvel Zombies, DCeased, and others) and publisher Salt Games are working with Max to bring him from his kitchen straight to your tabletop with a brand-new worker-placement game based on his popular series, which launched on Kickstarter this week. Recently, we had the chance to sit down with both Max and Michael to hear about how this new adaptation will play, a bit about how it all came to be, and why, whether you are coming at this as a fan of Tasting History or board games, there will be something on this plate you may like.

In Tasting History: The Board Game, each player works to collect ingredients from various locations on the board, which they use to cook and prepare delicious, historically accurate recipes. They host parties and progress through ages, watching the offerings grow with the passing of time. Featured in the base box will be three different historical periods, including ancient Rome, medieval Europe, and the American Frontier, each highlighting 25 unique recipes from the period and various historical events.

The game itself is split into five rounds, with 1-5 players taking turns placing their four chefs at the various spots on the era’s board, and is completed in only about 60-90 minutes. Each of the six main locations allows players to gather ingredients required to complete their recipes and provide other benefits. 

Additionally, players may collect special Insight cards, which Michael elaborated on: “[Insight Cards] are different little bonuses that let you cheat in some way or gain an advantage when the conditions are met. These can range from giving you free ingredients to giving you extra bonus victory points to letting you do things when other players move into your space and whatnot,” acting a bit as the “take that” mechanic in Tasting History that they describe as “forced assistance.”

In addition to their own boards, each of the three eras will feature period-authentic decks of cards to really help sell the showcase that time in history. These include decks of recipes to cook, events from the period that will serve as special goals each player can complete during the game--along with specifying their starting resources--and each era will have a special ingredient that, if played alongside the other requirements for a recipe, can gain you additional rewards. Rome, for example, will feature the fermented fish sauce garum, which Max previously did a whole episode on. 

It’s also with these eras that I have my biggest question marks and concerns. The fact that the base game comes with the three different boards, each with their own set of recipes, events, advancements, and more--many of which you won’t see every game--could give it a great amount of replayability. However, I worry that instead of feeling interesting and exciting to play in their own right, they will just feel like a reskin, swapping out Roman snails for cowboy beans. If you are going to pack in two extra boards and a couple hundred more cards to play with, I want there to be something that makes me excited to check them out. 

One thing that both Max and Michael made very clear is that it is designed to be a standalone board game, and it just so happens to be themed around Tasting History, meaning it can be enjoyed even if you don’t get the whole “hardtack” shtick. 

“It's all about the gameplay first,” Max explained. “I have played a lot of board games that are very on-theme for certain properties, and I've played them once and never had a desire to play it again because I think, ‘Oh, that was fun. Next.’ 

"My goal is to have a game along the lines of Wingspan [or] Lords of Waterdeep that I can play 50 times and enjoy it as much on the 50th time as the first time.” 

Don’t worry, though, fellow tasting historians--Max isn’t forgetting about you: “If you do watch the show and you're a big fan, there are so many little nods to the show specifically in this, [and] not only the fact that most of the recipes I have already done,” he said.

The idea is to incorporate the “history” aspect that is such a critical part of the show into this tabletop rendition. Max said, “We're working on possibly getting a way to actually link to those recipes within the game.” 

Michael elaborated on one idea being thrown around involving QR codes on the recipes: “For example, ‘Oh, I want to learn more about sweet and sour beef and why that's really cool in the setting.’ You just scan that with your phone and, boom, you get to watch, you know, 20 minutes of Max just talking about it immediately.” As someone who loves both the educational and cooking qualities of the show, I appreciate that it’s even being considered.

Both Max and Michael are well aware of the fine thread they are balancing, trying to make a game that can appeal to board gamers--offering them replayability, depth, and worthwhile decisions--and the channel's 4.5 million subscribers, who might be playing their first board game that isn’t Uno or Monopoly and need something approachable and fun. 

“We also want this [Tasting History] to be accessible,” Michael said. “Max happens to be a board gamer, but his audience is not necessarily a bunch of ravenous board gamers. So, we want this to have a level of accessibility.” 

Getting to that place, though, has been quite the adventure in and of itself. “Before I had first talked with Max, I was envisioning something like a Ticket to Ride or even a lower-level Catan... I say this affectionately, but like, baby's first board game for when people are coming [to] this from the mass-market stuff. Then after one conversation with Max where it's like, ‘Oh, he's an actual board gamer, and he wants this to be a board game first and foremost,’ that changed the entire direction of where the project went,” Michael revealed. These changes even include turning away from a cooperative experience in favor of the final competitive setup.

“One of the earlier versions of the game was that you had a communal feast [during which] you would draw every game that the players were trying to accomplish, but kind of competitively, communally together. You know, you got bonuses for completing it first, but the goal of the game was everyone was trying to complete it.” Michael explained. “It was more cooperative-leaning in that regard. The expression on Max's face when I said, ‘Now, we can make this full co-op...’I am sitting here assuming Max Miller, the learned, ‘I'm trying to spread knowledge and insights to the internet masses here,’ would be more like, ‘Let's all work together to complete a goal.’ And then he just goes like, ‘Oh no, no, no. I want this to be competitive.’” Michael chuckled, before Max chimed in with a laugh, “I'm not huge into co-op games. Once in a while, but I like winning!”

Swapping my Tasting History subscriber hat for my board-gamer one, hearing Max and Michael showcase Tasting History’s mechanisms and flow, I’m impressed with how well it seems to have come together to create that sort of approachable depth that other mass-market-appeal games like Wingspan or Ticket to Ride have. That said, I haven't played it yet, so how successful it is remains to be seen, but there are certainly qualities and designs here that would make me feel comfortable betting on their success. 

One example is not locking out a space just because someone else got there first. Much of Tasting History reminds me of Everdell (one of my wife’s and my own favorite games and one I would recommend anyone to play) with its worker-placement and time-progression aspects, but here, you can freely place a chef somewhere that is already occupied. That eliminates a good amount of the “meanness” that this could have had and makes the whole thing feel more approachable. Though some of those Insight cards will cause a bit of that “forced assistance,” it's not quite to the same detriment for the other player. Other considerations like simplified setup options are being included to further assist and give options to board-game newcomers, which should lower that barrier of entry even further.

For other interested historians and board-game aficionados, the folks at Salt Entertainment has a prototype mod of the game on the popular digital tabletop client Tabletop Simulator, which you can find over on Steam. Unfortunately, I don’t think the solo mode that lets you go up against Max himself will be included, which sounds like all sorts of fun. “Solo mode is currently in development, [in] which you'll be playing against Max Miller himself. We're currently balancing him because he went from being way too hard to being a little too easy, and now he's in a general good area. He does kind of cheat a little bit, but you know, that's kind of fun. He literally has his card where he just says, ‘I don't like the ingredients I have. I'm just going to clack some hardtack together and just improvise a recipe here,’” Michael laughed.

“Created for families, history lovers, food enthusiasts, and gamers alike” is one of the big slogans featured over on the game’s Kickstarter page. As someone who is a longtime fan of Tasting History and even longer a fan of board games, what Tasting History: The Board Game looks to deliver is a great choice both for a quick game after putting the kid down or at my next game night with my group of friends who tend to get competitive. Time will tell whether all the ingredients come together in a feast worthy of Ceasar, or something that would have been better served at Emperor Domitian's Feast of Death.

In addition to their own boards, each of the three eras will feature period-authentic decks of cards to really help sell the showcase that time in history. These include decks of recipes to cook, events from the period that will serve as special goals each player can complete during the game--along with specifying their starting resources--and each era will have a special ingredient that, if played alongside the other requirements for a recipe, can gain you additional rewards. Rome, for example, will feature the fermented fish sauce garum, which Max previously did a whole episode on. 

It’s also with these eras that I have my biggest question marks and concerns. The fact that the base game comes with the three different boards, each with their own set of recipes, events, advancements, and more--many of which you won’t see every game--could give it a great amount of replayability. However, I worry that instead of feeling interesting and exciting to play in their own right, they will just feel like a reskin, swapping out Roman snails for cowboy beans. If you are going to pack in two extra boards and a couple hundred more cards to play with, I want there to be something that makes me excited to check them out. 

One thing that both Max and Michael made very clear is that it is designed to be a standalone board game, and it just so happens to be themed around Tasting History, meaning it can be enjoyed even if you don’t get the whole “hardtack” shtick. 

“It's all about the gameplay first,” Max explained. “I have played a lot of board games that are very on-theme for certain properties, and I've played them once and never had a desire to play it again because I think, ‘Oh, that was fun. Next.’ 

"My goal is to have a game along the lines of Wingspan [or] Lords of Waterdeep that I can play 50 times and enjoy it as much on the 50th time as the first time.” 

Don’t worry, though, fellow tasting historians--Max isn’t forgetting about you: “If you do watch the show and you're a big fan, there are so many little nods to the show specifically in this, [and] not only the fact that most of the recipes I have already done,” he said.

The idea is to incorporate the “history” aspect that is such a critical part of the show into this tabletop rendition. Max said, “We're working on possibly getting a way to actually link to those recipes within the game.” 

Michael elaborated on one idea being thrown around involving QR codes on the recipes: “For example, ‘Oh, I want to learn more about sweet and sour beef and why that's really cool in the setting.’ You just scan that with your phone and, boom, you get to watch, you know, 20 minutes of Max just talking about it immediately.” As someone who loves both the educational and cooking qualities of the show, I appreciate that it’s even being considered.

Both Max and Michael are well aware of the fine thread they are balancing, trying to make a game that can appeal to board gamers--offering them replayability, depth, and worthwhile decisions--and the channel's 4.5 million subscribers, who might be playing their first board game that isn’t Uno or Monopoly and need something approachable and fun. 

“We also want this [Tasting History] to be accessible,” Michael said. “Max happens to be a board gamer, but his audience is not necessarily a bunch of ravenous board gamers. So, we want this to have a level of accessibility.” 

Getting to that place, though, has been quite the adventure in and of itself. “Before I had first talked with Max, I was envisioning something like a Ticket to Ride or even a lower-level Catan... I say this affectionately, but like, baby's first board game for when people are coming [to] this from the mass-market stuff. Then after one conversation with Max where it's like, ‘Oh, he's an actual board gamer, and he wants this to be a board game first and foremost,’ that changed the entire direction of where the project went,” Michael revealed. These changes even include turning away from a cooperative experience in favor of the final competitive setup.

“One of the earlier versions of the game was that you had a communal feast [during which] you would draw every game that the players were trying to accomplish, but kind of competitively, communally together. You know, you got bonuses for completing it first, but the goal of the game was everyone was trying to complete it.” Michael explained. “It was more cooperative-leaning in that regard. The expression on Max's face when I said, ‘Now, we can make this full co-op...’I am sitting here assuming Max Miller, the learned, ‘I'm trying to spread knowledge and insights to the internet masses here,’ would be more like, ‘Let's all work together to complete a goal.’ And then he just goes like, ‘Oh no, no, no. I want this to be competitive.’” Michael chuckled, before Max chimed in with a laugh, “I'm not huge into co-op games. Once in a while, but I like winning!”

Swapping my Tasting History subscriber hat for my board-gamer one, hearing Max and Michael showcase Tasting History’s mechanisms and flow, I’m impressed with how well it seems to have come together to create that sort of approachable depth that other mass-market-appeal games like Wingspan or Ticket to Ride have. That said, I haven't played it yet, so how successful it is remains to be seen, but there are certainly qualities and designs here that would make me feel comfortable betting on their success. 

One example is not locking out a space just because someone else got there first. Much of Tasting History reminds me of Everdell (one of my wife’s and my own favorite games and one I would recommend anyone to play) with its worker-placement and time-progression aspects, but here, you can freely place a chef somewhere that is already occupied. That eliminates a good amount of the “meanness” that this could have had and makes the whole thing feel more approachable. Though some of those Insight cards will cause a bit of that “forced assistance,” it's not quite to the same detriment for the other player. Other considerations like simplified setup options are being included to further assist and give options to board-game newcomers, which should lower that barrier of entry even further.

For other interested historians and board-game aficionados, the folks at Salt Entertainment has a prototype mod of the game on the popular digital tabletop client Tabletop Simulator, which you can find over on Steam. Unfortunately, I don’t think the solo mode that lets you go up against Max himself will be included, which sounds like all sorts of fun. “Solo mode is currently in development, [in] which you'll be playing against Max Miller himself. We're currently balancing him because he went from being way too hard to being a little too easy, and now he's in a general good area. He does kind of cheat a little bit, but you know, that's kind of fun. He literally has his card where he just says, ‘I don't like the ingredients I have. I'm just going to clack some hardtack together and just improvise a recipe here,’” Michael laughed.

“Created for families, history lovers, food enthusiasts, and gamers alike” is one of the big slogans featured over on the game’s Kickstarter page. As someone who is a longtime fan of Tasting History and even longer a fan of board games, what Tasting History: The Board Game looks to deliver is a great choice both for a quick game after putting the kid down or at my next game night with my group of friends who tend to get competitive. Time will tell whether all the ingredients come together in a feast worthy of Ceasar, or something that would have been better served at Emperor Domitian's Feast of Death.

title: The Halo We Grew Up With Is Never Coming Back
summary:
It has been less than two years since Xbox announced that longtime series developer 343 Industries would be rebranding to Halo Studios. This was envisioned as a new dawn for the beloved shooter franchise, as Xbox seemed to leave the Reclaimer Trilogy behind as it sought to tighten Master Chief’s focus to enable a more faithful and satisfying future.

As someone who always held out hope for Halo regardless of how dire things seemed, I was legitimately convinced that this reformed studio was destined for bigger and brighter things. I became even more reassured following the July release of Campaign Evolved, a confident remake that despite polarising reception amongst hardcore audiences, did its job of pulling a fading icon back into the limelight. If the next steps were carefully made, we could have been living in a reality where Halo took over the world again. 

But with Microsoft obliterating Halo Studios with 268 layoffs and putting the series’ future under the Activision umbrella, my fading flame has finally flickered out. Whatever form it takes in the coming years with a new team and a refreshed creative vision, I simply cannot bring myself to care anymore. The Halo I grew up with is gone, and the cheering I have done from the sidelines for all these years has been for nothing. 

I wish this weren’t the case, because there were so many moments over the years that oozed potential. Halo 4 dove into more compelling lore than Bungie ever did, while it was amazing to watch 343 Industries flesh Master Chief out into more than a stoic naval officer. He is far more complex: a child soldier bred for warfare and robbed of personal agency so much that the only meaningful relationship he has is with an artificial intelligence destined to eventually leave him behind. 

Unfortunately, the potential of this storyline was abandoned when Xbox decided to soft-reboot the franchise with Halo Infinite: a game that was intended to--as the name suggests--grow into an eternal home for all things Halo. Its free-to-play multiplayer had the potential to rival huge live-service efforts like Fortnite or Destiny, but a glacial approach to seasonal updates and its failure to maintain an active audience led to a premature demise.

As for the campaign, the presumed events of a nonexistent Halo 6 took place offscreen as we reunite with Chief long after the battle has been lost. Once again, a narrative examination of how this once-unstoppable soldier deals with picking up the remnants of a human race he was expected to save is incredibly powerful. All of those opportunities to produce something wonderful, lasting, and impactful never quite reached their full potential. Much has been uncovered about how things turned out this way, and many of the internal decisions made were a foolish attempt to try to recapture what Halo used to be. It was a dominant global titan that transformed the medium time and time again as it pushed the shooter genre to new heights, gave people a reason to sign up for Xbox Live, and helped the platform stay afloat during an awkward start--but that's no longer the case. 

Bungie’s original trilogy was lightning in a bottle. Three masterful games released over the course of seven years that would go on to define an entire generation of culture. I’m not exaggerating when I say millions of gamers were raised by Halo. It helped define several of my own tastes during a formative time in my life as I played through each story campaign with my older brother and felt like I was taking part in a living, breathing battle: a conflict that was confident in its mechanical and narrative ambitions despite having to live up to massive expectations. It stuck the landing each and every time, with ODST and Reach acting as big ol’ cherries on top before the series was finally laid to rest. Or so we thought.

We hold the first three games to such an untouchable standard because of what they came to represent: experiences that evolved the medium before our eyes while bringing countless gamers together in a world before social media and smartphones. There was something so intimately raw about fighting alongside Master Chief with close friends under the dim light of a cracking CRT display. The medium we know today was still finding its feet in a brand-new era, and Halo played a fundamental part in that journey. Fondness in the moment has since morphed into entrenched nostalgia, which is precisely what Xbox has been trying again and again to recapture to mixed results. Not the gameplay or narrative, since 343 Industries has done an admirable job of taking risks in that department, but rather the emotions Halo once stirred up inside of us all those years ago. 

But things change, and video games no longer exist in a landscape where a game like Halo can waltz along and take over the world. We have become accustomed to live-service titans like Fortnite and Call of Duty, which have thrown aside traditional solo campaigns and online multiplayer in favour of something alien. 

Our present is about platforms making lots of money and sinking their hooks into players for as long as possible rather than offering an adventure that stays with you. The original Halo trilogy made and tried to do things within the medium that had never been done before, which is precisely what made them so memorable to an entire generation. Whether you were a player or a developer, we were all watching this magic come to life at the exact same time. 

As much as it breaks my heart to admit this, it’s time to stop hoping for Xbox to somehow recapture this unattainable magic. For the past two decades we have watched brave new stories dropped unceremoniously and gameplay changes introduced as the giant tries to achieve the impossible. We finished the fight back on Xbox 360, and this fruitless chase of trying to justify a new conflict has given us nothing but manufactured nostalgia. I love Halo, but it’s finally time to let it go.

title: Star Wars Battlefront 3 Reportedly In Development By EA’s Top Shooter Studios
summary:
Included in the shocking news of EA's restructuring, which includes layoffs and the closure of BioWare, is a mention from the publisher that Apex Legends studio Respawn Entertainment and Battlefield maker DICE are collaborating on a project. According to a report, that project is a long-awaited sequel set in a galaxy far, far away.

Per Variety, which cites "multiple sources," the DICE and Respawn project is Star Wars Battlefront 3. While EA itself did not confirm this, the company's memo about the restructuring says that the studios' title will contribute to EA's goal of delivering a "shooter portfolio that unlocks growth."

EA specifically states that learnings from Battlefield 6's launch and live service will further that goal, while also announcing that Apex Legends will be expanded with new "gameplay modes" and "other new experiences."

As for the purported existence of Star Wars Battlefront 3, the timing coincides with a recent rumor that Lucasfilm Games was seeking a development partner for a new Battlefront, and that DICE and Sony-owned studio Bungie were among the studios being considered.

DICE had made two Star Wars Battlefront games for EA, which were released in 2015 and 2017. Battlefront 2 attracted criticism over loot boxes (remember when that was the hot controversy of the day?), but the game still proved to be massively popular. Last year, Battlefront 2 suddenly had a resurgence in players, with many hoping that it would ignite talks of a third Battlefront.

Outside of Battlefront and shooters, the Star Wars franchise has gained two new popular entries this year alone, with strategy game Star Wars Zero Company (which Respawn co-developed) and racing title Star Wars: Galactic Racer enjoying critical success.

title: Xbox Cloud Gaming Hourly Prices Revealed For Non-Game Pass Members
summary:
Microsoft has revealed how much it will charge people for using the Xbox Cloud Gaming service without a Game Pass membership. Right now, this is available only to Xbox Insiders, but that's a free program that anyone can join.

Also notable is that the prices below are described as "introductory launch pricing," and that wording suggests the prices may change in the future. Microsoft is calling these "cloud playtime packs."

Cloud playtime packs pricing:

  • 10 hours for $4
  • 25 hours for $8
  • 50 hours for $12

Anyone who buys these cloud playtime packs will get access to cloud gaming without ads and with perks like shorter wait times and higher-quality streaming. These packs will be available to more people starting in November.

A version of Xbox cloud gaming with ads is also available to Xbox Insiders without a Game Pass membership.

As for those who do have a Game Pass membership, changes are coming to cloud gaming in November. Microsoft will put limits on how many hours per month people can use the service, and then allow people to pay more to unlock more time. Below is a breakdown of how many hours you’ll get included with the tier of Game Pass you’re subscribed to:

  • Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours
  • Game Pass Premium: 10 hours
  • Game Pass Essential: 5 hours

Microsoft said it understands this is a “meaningful change,” especially for those who use the cloud regularly for gaming. However, the company said it estimates that these changes will impact about 4% of Game Pass subscribers, though the company did not share any specifics on how it arrived at that projection.

In other Game Pass news, it was recently reported that Xbox CEO Asha Sharma is considering a massive shakeup to the service to allow people to build their own Game Pass and choose which features they do and do not want.

title: Don’t Worry, You’re Not The Only One Dying Too Much In Modern Warfare 4’s Campaign
summary:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 releases this week, and the campaign and DMZ are currently in early access. Infinity Ward delivers an epic series conclusion for its Modern Warfare reboot, but if you're finding some missions tough on a normal difficulty setting, don't worry–you're not alone.

Modern Warfare 4 features 16 missions in total, and these offer a wide variety of staple Call of Duty missions, such as stealth ops, cinematic chase sequences, and a slow-motion breach-and-clear scenario. There are also a couple of intense melee-style boss fights, where your life depends on well-timed parrying.

As a longtime Call of Duty player who typically plays through all the campaigns on both normal and veteran difficulties, Modern Warfare 4's normal difficulty feels tougher than what we've experienced in the last few years. This takes me back to Infinity Ward's most recent game, Modern Warfare 2, when the NPCs also felt like much more formidable opponents. It was easy to underestimate the AI's ability to overwhelm you, and they always seemed just smart enough to sniff you out during stealth missions. 

The NPCs aren't necessarily more intelligent in Modern Warfare 4, but they do feel like they are buffed up and shooting straighter this year, so trying to rush through their defenses can be unwise. I was humbled more than a few times when trying to clear out an area with a large presence of enemy soldiers, and I had to repeat one of the boss fights more than I'd like to admit. I've heard this same complaint from others playing Modern Warfare 4's campaign, so surely this isn't an age or skill issue, but Infinity Ward delivering another challenging campaign.

Overall, Modern Warfare 4 on normal difficulty isn't too painful and definitely a manageable setting to play on, but it has forced me to play slower and show more patience. I'll still give the campaign a try on the veteran setting, but that's the highest challenge I'm aiming for. For those eager for an ultimate test of skill, Modern Warfare 4 introduces a "YOLO" difficulty setting, which requires you to restart the entire campaign if you die.

Modern Warfare 4 fully releases on October 23 for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, PC, and Switch 2.

title: EA Shuts Down Dragon Age, Mass Effect Studio BioWare
summary:
Publisher Electronic Arts is planning to shut down legendary RPG studio BioWare, laying off about 50 employees at the studio alongside 350 more elsewhere.

In a new Bloomberg report, a person familiar with the matter said a total of 3% of EA's overall company has been affected by this latest round of layoffs.

BioWare posted a statement to X, confirming that it's shutting down and thanking everyone for their support over the studio's lifetime. It's quite a sad day.

"There is nothing easy about writing these words," BioWare said. "Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition. What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own."

In a staff letter sent out on Wednesday that has now been shared by the company, EA chief operating officer David Tinson and chief studios officer Cam Weber explained that the company took a "hard look" at its business over the last several months. This resulted in some projects getting canceled, including the next Mass Effect game--which was in early development at BioWare--as well as a planned game in The Sims franchise codenamed Project Lotus. Instead, the resources allocated to that title will be diverted to something else currently codenamed Project Evergreen.

Many of EA's currently released franchises will continue as expected. Full Circle will keep working on Skate, but EA said the team there would be downsized. Meanwhile, its myriad sports games, Apex Legends, Battlefield, the next Star Wars Jedi game, and a new game based on Iron Man will continue to be invested in.

"Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," Tinson and Weber wrote in the letter.

This comes one year after EA agreed to a buyout by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund for $55 billion and two months after the company went private following the acquisition. The writing was on the wall, however, as EA told investors in March that it planned to save some $700 million after the massive leveraged buyout saddled the company with billions of dollars in debt.

The studio needs no introduction, but BioWare is quite the storied developer. Founded in February 1995, the Canadian studio is known for its many RPGs from Baldur's Gate and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic to Dragon Age and Mass Effect. Things haven't been too successful for BioWare recently, though, with both 2019's Anthem and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to meet expectations. While Mass Effect 5 has been in development since at least February 2022, that project is dead ... and so is BioWare.

BioWare posted a statement to X, confirming that it's shutting down and thanking everyone for their support over the studio's lifetime. It's quite a sad day.

"There is nothing easy about writing these words," BioWare said. "Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition. What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own."

In a staff letter sent out on Wednesday that has now been shared by the company, EA chief operating officer David Tinson and chief studios officer Cam Weber explained that the company took a "hard look" at its business over the last several months. This resulted in some projects getting canceled, including the next Mass Effect game--which was in early development at BioWare--as well as a planned game in The Sims franchise codenamed Project Lotus. Instead, the resources allocated to that title will be diverted to something else currently codenamed Project Evergreen.

Many of EA's currently released franchises will continue as expected. Full Circle will keep working on Skate, but EA said the team there would be downsized. Meanwhile, its myriad sports games, Apex Legends, Battlefield, the next Star Wars Jedi game, and a new game based on Iron Man will continue to be invested in.

"Across our portfolio, we're making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth," Tinson and Weber wrote in the letter.

This comes one year after EA agreed to a buyout by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund for $55 billion and two months after the company went private following the acquisition. The writing was on the wall, however, as EA told investors in March that it planned to save some $700 million after the massive leveraged buyout saddled the company with billions of dollars in debt.

The studio needs no introduction, but BioWare is quite the storied developer. Founded in February 1995, the Canadian studio is known for its many RPGs from Baldur's Gate and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic to Dragon Age and Mass Effect. Things haven't been too successful for BioWare recently, though, with both 2019's Anthem and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to meet expectations. While Mass Effect 5 has been in development since at least February 2022, that project is dead ... and so is BioWare.

title: Rayman Legends Retold’s New Baguette Costumes Are A Tip Of The Beret To Expedition 33
summary:
Rayman Legends Retold is almost here, and as you'd expect from this remake, it's a pretty noticeable graphical glow-up of Rayman Legends and it includes a very French outfit for you to dress the phantom-limbed hero and his partner Barbara up in. Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 fans, this is where you do the Leonardo DiCaprio pointing meme.

Even though Ubisoft doesn't mention Sandfall Interactive or Expedition 33 by name, it did confirm that the new baguette outfits are "a playful nod to a fellow game" created in Montpellier. "Conceived as a tribute from one French studio to another, these costumes celebrate the creativity, passion, and unmistakably French touch that continue to make the country's video game industry shine on the global stage," Ubisoft said in a press release. Sandfall Interactive is also headquartered in Montpellier.

The friendly homage is no doubt a tribute to Sandfall Interactive and its award-winning debut game, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. The Expedition 33 outfit features a white shirt with black pinstripes, black pants with black suspenders, a red beret, and a baguette kept inside a red-and-white plaid cloth, making it as Gallic as Groundskeeper Willie's introduction to the beautiful French language. Unlocking the outfit for each character in the hit RPG isn't easy, as players must defeat secret mime mini-bosses around the map.

The look isn't unique to either game, as the ensemble draws on 19th-century naval uniforms, Basque headwear, and "Onion Johnny" door-to-door traders. Over time, those fashion elements became synonymous with France, becoming a symbol of French elegance and casual style that artists like Pablo Picasso and fashion icon Jean Paul Gaultier adopted. You've probably also spotted people wearing these costumes at conventions, as Expedition 33's baguette outfits make for an easy, low-cost, and comfortable cosplay.

Ubisoft says the baguette costumes will be available to all players at launch, when the game launches for PC, PS5, Xbox Series X|S, and Switch 2 on December 3. It's the second big remake from Ubisoft this year, following the release of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced in July.

title: Another Day, Another Pokemon Card Heist Worth Nearly $1 Million
summary:
I guess someone's gotta collect 'em all, and it appears that thieves are doing just that, as yet another high-stakes burglary in Southern California has resulted in just about $1 million worth of Pokemon cards being stolen from a FedEx truck.

According to a report by The New York Times' sports journalism department, The Athletic (via ABC News), a FedEx truck parked near the authenticating and grading business known as the Professional Sports Authenticator in Santa Ana, California, was robbed on October 13. The Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement to ABC News that hundreds of cards were stolen, with the robbery estimated at a value of $963,000.

"The pallets contained various trading cards, including, but not limited to, sports cards and Pokemon cards," the Santa Ana Police Department said in a statement. "However, the exact value of the stolen items has not yet been determined."

According to the Santa Ana Police Department, the thieves broke into the FedEx truck, stole two full pallets of cards, and tore through a third pallet for even more packaged goodies--all of which belonged to collectors from across the country who submitted their cards to the Professional Sports Authenticator to be authenticated and graded for collecting or reselling purposes.

Collectors, the parent company of the Professional Sports Authenticator, told ABC News that in the wake of the theft, it has deactivated the certificates for the missing cards and notified its other businesses in its marketplace to "be on the lookout" for the cards in case they turn up.

"We are aware of a theft involving a third-party shipping vehicle carrying PSA-graded items," the company said. "We are working closely with law enforcement and the carrier as the investigation continues. Our customer service team has contacted affected customers directly and is arranging compensation based on fair market value. We understand the impact this has on collectors involved, many of whom see these cards as far more than a financial asset."

FedEx is also aware of the burglary, telling ABC News that it's cooperating with police.

"The security of our customers' shipments is a top priority, and we are working with local law enforcement in their investigation," the corporation said. "Further questions should be referred to local investigators."

This seems to be a regular occurrence these days: people stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of Pokemon cards, sometimes at gunpoint. What was once a fun hobby has become quite fraught as people battle each other to get their hands on cards. I don't know what happened because it wasn't like this 30 years ago, but soon, you may need a face just to buy Pokemon cards. Yikes.
